primary_claim: Directly optimizing a feature label via token-space gradient descent, using an LLM as a differentiable discriminator rather than a hypothesis generator, converges to correct single-token labels for several synthetic toy features (animal, Chinese text, number, and mammal under balanced sampling), but defaults to broader categories under unbalanced sampling and fails when the base model cannot reliably classify the concept (e.g. palindromes).

effect.metric: label-convergence success across tested synthetic features
effect.value: converged to the correct single-token label for animal, Chinese, number, and mammal (balanced sampling); failed to find the correct label for mammal under unbalanced natural-text sampling (defaulted to 'animal') and for palindrome detection (defaulted to 'a')

stated_future_work: optimize sequences of multiple tokens instead of single-token labels to express more complex concepts
address the tendency to default to broader categories for hierarchical/insufficiently-distinguished categories with more sophisticated sampling strategies
address failure cases where the evaluation model can't reliably classify instances of a feature even when given the correct label
reduce the human intervention currently needed to tune hyperparameters for different features
limitations_stated: currently only optimizes single-token labels, limiting the complexity of expressible concepts
without balanced sampling, hierarchical/narrower categories default to the broader category (e.g. mammal collapses to animal)
method fails when the evaluation LLM can't reliably classify instances of a feature even given the correct label (e.g. palindromes)
method can be finicky about the hyperparameters under which it works, so it's not yet very robust
requires human intervention to tune hyperparameters for different features
quote: The method successfully labeled features like "animal," "mammal," "Chinese," and "number" in our proof-of-concept experiments
